newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole embark on final campaign sprints.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole embark on final campaign sprints.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole embarked on final campaign trips on Wednesday, urging supporters to get out and vote next Tuesday knowing turnout could decide which party controls Congress.
Both Clinton and Dole left Washington, aiming to stay on the road for the final six days of the campaign until the November 5 election, after which one will return the winner.

Clinton headed for Michigan, Colorado and Arizona while Dole flew to Tennessee. The Dole schedule was being worked out on a day-to-day basis, as strategists and the candidate himself tried to figure out where he could best use his time.

The latest Reuters tracking poll showed Clinton's lead shrinking to single digits for the first time since October 24. He led Dole by 9.8 percentage points as the number of undecided voters rose above 13 percent. But Dole's support remained stuck at 33 percent -- hardly an encouraging sign.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's support was now above the eight percent mark, having risen by three points in the past week.
Other polling organisations put Clinton's lead at between 12 and 19 points, pointing to a possible landslide.
With the presidential race seemingly a foregone conclusion, attention has switched to a tight battle for control of Congress, which the Republicans won two years ago for the first time in 40 years.

A Reuters survey of 34 political scientists around the country found that two thirds thought the Republicans would hold their 53-47 majority in the Senate roughly unchanged and also keep a wafer-thin edge in the House of Representatives, where they now have a 38-seat majority.
"It will depend on weather and turnout. Dame Fortuna will tip the balance," said Lief Carter of Colorado College in Colorado Springs.
Both Clinton and Dole have been exhorting their supporters to come out and vote. Many experts believe turnout will be relatively low after an uninspiring presidential campaign.

High voter participation is usually thought to benefit Democrats but Dole's failure to energise his own supporters could depress Republican turnout in any case and hurt his party's candidates all the way down the ticket.
Polls show the struggle for Congress to be extremely close with many House Republicans who swept into office on the 1994 anti-Clinton surge now struggling for survival.
But recent polls in some key Senate races show Republicans gaining ground, leading analysts to believe that the party's grip on the Senate will not be seriously challenged.
Dole has found an issue in challenging the Democrats on taking questionable campaign contributions from financial interests in Indonesia and elsewhere in Asia.

An embarrassed Democratic Party on Tuesday tried to defuse a crisis over alleged campaign financing violations by sending the Federal Elections Commission a draft report on donations it had planned to file only after the election. The report had been due last week. The Democrats acted only after the Republicans said they would ask a federal court for an injunction to freeze all Democratic spending.
Republican Chairman Haley Barbour said Wednesday there was a "rotten stench" emanating from the White House and the Democratic Committee which came from Clinton's "flagrant violations of the law."

Clinton aides said he hoped to turn the tables on his rival with a major campaign speech, possibly on Thursday, accusing Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Dole of standing in the way of campaign finance reform.
